questions.question: Describe factory farming, with South African examples, and evaluate its benefits and costs.
questions.expected_answer: Intensive livestock farming: many animals in confined spaces (sheds, cages, pens), factory methods, cheapest production; vs extensive/free-range. Developed after WWII (automation, vaccines, antibiotics, breeding). SA: poultry largest sector; broilers in climate-controlled sheds of tens of thousands, market weight in about 5-6 weeks, maize/soy feed; battery-caged layers (some cage-free); pigs indoors; most beef cattle finished in feedlots (Free State, North West, Gauteng, Northern Cape). Benefits: affordable protein, efficient land use, consistency, jobs, demand for grain. Costs: welfare (crowding, natural behaviour, leg and heart problems; SPCA; EU cage ban), antibiotic resistance, disease spread (bird flu culls 2023), manure pollution and eutrophication, smells, feed land/water/energy, methane emissions, corporate dominance, imports.

questions.question: Explain what genetically modified crops are and how they are used in South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Genes = DNA instructions; selective breeding over millennia (maize from teosinte); genetic modification changes DNA directly, often inserting genes from other species; GMO. Traits: Bt insect resistance (Bacillus thuringiensis protein toxic to stalk borer), herbicide tolerance; drought tolerance; Golden Rice (beta-carotene, vitamin A). SA: Bt cotton late 1990s, Bt maize 1998; GMO Act 1997 risk assessment; largest GM grower in Africa; most maize, soybeans, cotton GM; eaten daily in maize meal.

questions.question: Discuss the arguments for and against genetically modified crops.
questions.expected_answer: For: higher yields, fewer insecticide sprays, supports no-till conservation agriculture, drought-tolerant and nutrient-enriched varieties, WHO and science academies find approved GM foods as safe as conventional. Against: gene flow and biodiversity, resistance (SA stalk borer within about a decade; refuges; herbicide-resistant weeds), patents and corporate control, buying seed each season, dependence for small farmers, hunger caused by poverty, labelling and right to know (Consumer Protection Act), ethical/religious objections. Balanced: effects depend on crop, trait, management and control; regulation, independent research, resistance management, fair access, clear information.
